Shocks to public debt maturity and effect on the macroeconomy
abstract: Over the last few decades, there has been substantial variation in the average maturity at which US government debt is issued. More recently, in the face of rising debt-to-GDP, it is important to analyse whether the maturity at which a government funds its debt has implications on the macroeconomy. In this project, I use a novel design combining high-frequency data and institutional features of Treasury announcements in the primary market, to identify shocks to the maturity structure of US public debt. An exogenous increase in the maturity of new public debt issuance increases the term spread significantly, increases output, reduces unemployment steadily until a 1 year period, and leads to a persistent increase in inflation. I propose to calibrate a model embedding the preferred habitat framework in a New Keynesian model to analyse the transmission from bond supply to asset prices and to the macroeconomy.

Richer earnings dynamics, consumption and portfolio choice over the life cycle
abstract: Households face earnings risk which is non-normal and varies by age and over the income distribution. We show that allowing for these rich features of earnings dynamics, in the context of a structurally estimated life-cycle portfolio choice model, helps to better understand the limited participation of households in the stock market and their low holdings of risky assets. Because households are subject to more background risk than previously considered, the estimated model implies a substantially lower coefficient of risk aversion and a lower optimal risky share for older workers with low wealth and high earnings.
